paras: The Pulaski camp meeting raid was an attack by white deputy sheriffs on a large Black camp meeting at Pulaski, Georgia, reported under a July 4, 1919, dateline. The deputies beat many people about the head, several persons were shot, and with the help of white men from the community the meeting was broken up and prisoners were taken to the county seat. The Chicago Defender ran the story on its front page and compared it to an earlier deputies' action at Millen, Georgia.

The camp meeting celebrated a church anniversary. Among those selling refreshments was Robert Rhodes, a barber from Statesboro who had come to earn "a little extra change" at a lemonade stand with his helper, Cooper Williams.

According to the dispatch, white deputy sheriffs of "Chandler county" searched the refreshment stands and put their hands into the lemonade tubs, setting off a panic. The correspondent wrote that "many heads" were "battered with blunt weapons" and that several persons were shot. When the deputies reached the Rhodes stand, revolvers were fired, and Rhodes and Williams fought back by throwing peanuts, fish sandwiches and other goods from the stand.

The deputies then called on white men of the community for help, and within a few hours the meeting had been broken up. Several automobiles loaded with prisoners were driven to the county seat, printed as "Mt. Levi."
The dispatch names neither the prisoners nor the injured and gives no charges; no report of a hearing or inquiry appears in the coverage.

The only account found is a Century News Service dispatch that the Chicago Defender printed on page one of its July 5, 1919, issue. The correspondent called the deputies "indiscriminate" and described them combing "their dirty hands through the lemonade." Under subheads such as "Battle Officers" and "Deputies Call Help," the story told the stand keepers' resistance in mock-heroic terms, saying they "declared war on the deputies." It closed by likening the raid to an earlier, apparently deadly, action by deputies at Millen, Georgia, in a garbled passage.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Century News Service)
accounts.gist: White deputies raided the refreshment stands at a Black camp meeting, causing a panic, beating many and shooting several; with help from white men they broke up the meeting and took prisoners to the county seat.

The paper prints 'Chandler county'; the record's Candler is a reading of that spelling, not stated in the text
White deputy sheriffs of the county, joined by white men of the community
Officers (deputy sheriffs), later aided by white civilians
Attendees were not in custody when attacked; several carloads were then taken prisoner
Robert Rhodes and Cooper Williams named as stand keepers who fought the deputies; the beaten and shot are unnamed
